Nightmares — the extract

Read the full passage or listen to the supplied MP3
Ready
0:00 0:00

The account given below is a description of a recurring nightmare. This nightmare was a frequent occurrence when the author was ten or eleven years of age. The author often woke screaming and had to be calmed by parents.

It began again.

I was standing in bright sunshine on a hilltop. The hill stood on a perfectly flat plain. The hill was clothed in bright, uniformly green grass, as short as if it had been closely mown or cropped by vast numbers of rabbits. The sky above was a crisp, clean blue, with a few baguette clouds, like a painting by Magritte.

I stood with arms outstretched, as if crucified, turning slowly with the delicate breeze that wafted across the hill. As I turned, I hummed quietly and contentedly. Below me the patchwork patterns of fields circled, creating the feeling of a fairground ride.

The lazy feeling of the moment began to diminish. The quiet humming seemed to be fragmenting.

I was distracted by the sudden movement of a shadow on the ground before me. There was something behind me. I glanced over my shoulder in trepidation. There was something.

Fear surged from my stomach to lodge in my throat. I wanted desperately to scream but couldn’t. My mouth was choked by my own hand, crammed against my teeth. A vast wheel dwarfed me as I cringed on the ground, its shadow swallowing the hillside below. Its spokes were as bright as spears, rotating towards me. They glinted with evil.

I knew without doubt that the wheel threatened my entire existence. I was insignificant: I was miniscule. The wheel intimidated me. I tried to scurry away round the side of the wheel but to my horror, as I scampered, it turned to match my movements. Its motions were inevitable. It was menacing and overpowering. It mirrored my every move.

I began to struggle backwards, down the slope, on my backside. My one thought was to escape the doom that this wheel symbolised. Yet, as I scrambled back, the wheel began to advance towards me. I spun around and lurched to my feet. Staggering, I headed down the hillside. Before my eyes the patchwork of fields began to expand. The boundaries spread apart, like an opening sunshade. The fields were threatening to absorb me. Assaulted by another terror, I hesitated. I was caught between the wheel and the threat of being swallowed by the landscape.

Turning again, I stood in the darkness of the wheel’s immense shadow. As I looked up, the wheel seemed to rise and rise into the sky. My head strained backwards as I tried to see the top of the wheel. The back of my neck was compressed and my throat was stretched tautly, as I peered up and up. The wheel loomed over me and then seemed to swoop down on me.

In the abandonment of panic, I spun and fled. My arms were stretched out from my sides, like wings or sails, as if I could escape by flying away. But I was no Icarus! Behind me, the wheel began to gather speed. As I ran, I glanced first over one shoulder, then over the other. No matter how fast I ran, the wheel was gaining on me. As it increased its speed, the sense of fatality grew in me. I ran. My lungs were flexing like bellows. My heart pumped frantically in my ears. My legs thudded cyclically on the turf. My knees threatened to dissolve into gel: muscles, tendons and ligaments snapping like rubber bands.

The gentle humming that had started on the top of the hill was now a stereophonic dirge. The bass line was my terrified heartbeat. The melody was a cacophony of wailing voices, out of syncopation. The voices were attuned to the whirling gyrations of the wheel, as it pursued me down the hillside.

As exhaustion overtook me, my stride faltered. I felt in danger of being overrun by the wheel’s hurtling progress. I felt the tyreless rim of the wheel begin to touch my back. At first, delicately, then with the sharp, stomach-wrenching pain of flesh being parted, I felt wetness slide towards my waistband. My back was red, my vision blurred. Impelled by fear, I surged ever downwards, striving to keep a few centimetres ahead of the wheel.

Still, I could not cry or scream. Still, my throat was constricted. My breaths were short, sobbing gasps of air, sucked in desperately. It was no good, I could not breathe, I could not cry, I could not outrun this doom. My fate was sealed; there was no way out. I was going to be overtaken. I would be crushed. I would be left, a ridged and bloodied pulp, on the smooth grass slope. I would be impaled, speared on the spokes that spiked the air above me.

I felt myself dragged downwards by the enormous weight of my head. My arms windmilled around me. My legs concertinaed beneath me. I fell headlong. I tucked and I rolled, whirling over and over. I became a small ball of fear, bounding to destruction. As I pounded down on to the plain below the hill, I unfolded and flattened. With a thud, the air was blasted from my lungs by the impact. At that instant, the wailing choir of noise reached its crescendo. Upside down, I saw a momentary vision of the wheel’s rim, in extreme close-up. As metal pulverised flesh, I screamed at last. All was blackness!

Then the light dazzled me. My father put his arm around my shuddering shoulders and said, ‘Wake up, son. It’s all right. Was it the same dream again?’

Writing — recounting a personal experience

Text level work from the supplied page
The opening paragraphs give clues that the central character’s situation is not real. The page identifies two clues: the clouds look like a painting and the scenery has a fairground feeling. These create a mood that prepares the reader for the nightmare.

Clue 1

“a few baguette clouds, like a painting by Magritte”

Clue 2

“creating the feeling of a fairground ride”

Your response

How do these opening clues prepare the reader for the nightmare to come?

Vocabulary match

Dictionary and contextual work
Match each word from the supplied list to a meaning. Use Hint if you are unsure. When you check or reveal an answer, the guide explains why the meaning fits the passage.

Spelling — prefixes

Separate the prefix from the root word
Remember: a prefix is added at the beginning of a word. A root is the main word-part carrying the central idea. Use Hint before revealing if you are stuck. The uploaded page does not include a published answer key, so these are suggested classroom splits for this exercise. Some words are tricky: the remaining root may be an older word-part or the word may also contain a suffix such as -ed, -ing or -ly.

Grammar and punctuation — sentence types

Statements · questions · exclamations
The supplied page asks you to change each sentence into the other sentence types and to use the correct capital letters and punctuation.

Quick identify

Transform the sentence

Statement: You would hate this nightmare.

Question: Would you hate this nightmare?
Why: a question asks something, so would moves to the front and the sentence ends with ?

Exclamation: You would hate this nightmare!
Why: the word order can stay the same, but the strong feeling is shown with !

Original page tasks

1. Write three statements about the dream passage.

2. Write three questions you would want to ask the dreamer.

3. Write three exclamations that you might have made while being told about the dream by a friend, and indicate where in the passage you would have made each exclamation.
